claim: Open Science has changed research by making data accessible and shareable, contributing to replicability to accelerate and disseminate knowledge.
source: Open Science has changed research by making data accessible and shareable, contributing to replicability to accelerate and disseminate knowledge.
evidence: This is a general statement about Open Science principles that is part of established scientific knowledge and consensus in the research community.

claim: For rodent cognitive studies the availability of tools to share and disseminate data is scarce.
source: However, for rodent cognitive studies the availability of tools to share and disseminate data is scarce.
evidence: This is an assertion about the current state of the field based on the authors' knowledge and observation of available resources.

claim: Automated touchscreen-based tests enable systematic cognitive assessment with easily standardised outputs that can facilitate data dissemination.
source: Automated touchscreen-based tests enable systematic cognitive assessment with easily standardised outputs that can facilitate data dissemination.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about touchscreen testing methods and is further supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The manuscript presents an integration of touchscreen cognitive testing with an open-access database public repository (mousebytes.ca).
source: Here we present an integration of touchscreen cognitive testing with an open-access database public repository (mousebytes.ca), as well as a Web platform for knowledge dissemination (https://touchscreencognition.org).
evidence: This is a direct statement about what the authors have developed and presented in this work.

claim: The manuscript presents a Web platform for knowledge dissemination (https://touchscreencognition.org).
source: Here we present an integration of touchscreen cognitive testing with an open-access database public repository (mousebytes.ca), as well as a Web platform for knowledge dissemination (https://touchscreencognition.org).
evidence: This is a direct statement about what the authors have developed and presented in this work.

claim: The manuscript presents the largest dataset of age-dependent high-level cognitive assessment of mouse models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: We complement these resources with the largest dataset of age-dependent high-level cognitive assessment of mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, expanding knowledge of affected cognitive domains from male and female mice of three strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the extensive data collection described in the manuscript (652 mice, 62,411 xml files).

claim: The dataset expands knowledge of affected cognitive domains from male and female mice of three strains.
source: We complement these resources with the largest dataset of age-dependent high-level cognitive assessment of mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, expanding knowledge of affected cognitive domains from male and female mice of three strains.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript testing three mouse strains (3xTG-AD, 5xFAD, APP/PS1) of both sexes.

claim: Open Science initiatives featuring increased data sharing and high-throughput automated data collection have increased the efficiency, quality, integrity and reproducibility of data gathering over the past 10 years.
source: Over the past 10 years, Open Science initiatives featuring increased data sharing and high-throughput automated data collection have increased the efficiency, quality, integrity and reproducibility of data gathering (Johnson and O'Donnell, 2009; Rahman and Watabe, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson and O'Donnell, 2009 and Rahman and Watabe, 2018.

claim: In genomics, researchers have made major progress in understanding the genetic basis of diseases by establishing multi-research site consortia and by providing access to these data through different open repositories.
source: In genomics, for example, researchers have made major progress in understanding the genetic basis of diseases by establishing multi-research site consortia and by providing access to these data through different open repositories (Boucas, 2018; Diehl and Boyle, 2016; Gerstein, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boucas, 2018; Diehl and Boyle, 2016; and Gerstein, 2012.

claim: In neuroimaging, data sharing and large open-access databases have enabled the development of new analytic tools allowing researchers to address questions that could not be answered using single data sets.
source: In neuroimaging, data sharing and large open-access databases have enabled the development of new analytic tools allowing researchers to address questions that could not be answered using single data sets (Biswal et al., 2010; Poldrack and Gorgolewski, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Biswal et al., 2010 and Poldrack and Gorgolewski, 2014.

claim: The Jackson Laboratory has developed the Mouse Phenome Database, a repository of mouse data taken from several studies.
source: The Jackson Laboratory has developed the Mouse Phenome Database, a repository of mouse data taken from several studies (Grubb et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grubb et al., 2009.

claim: Resources such as the International Mouse Phenotyping Resource of Standardised Screens provide different pipelines for the characterisation of mouse lines.
source: Additionally, resources such as the International Mouse Phenotyping Resource of Standardised Screens provide different pipelines for the characterisation of mouse lines (Koscielny et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koscielny et al., 2014.

claim: Existing databases provide only limited information on high-level cognitive testing in mouse models.
source: Although these databases represent a necessary and fundamental shift in the availability of data, these repositories provide only limited information on high-level cognitive testing in mouse models.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the authors' knowledge of existing databases and their limitations.

claim: Conventional cognitive assessments in mouse models are subject to large variation.
source: Conventional cognitive assessments in mouse models are subject to large variation (Kafkafi et al., 2018; Wahlsten et al., 2003), which may be in part the result of lack of automation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kafkafi et al., 2018 and Wahlsten et al., 2003.

claim: Large variation in conventional cognitive assessments may be in part the result of lack of automation.
source: Conventional cognitive assessments in mouse models are subject to large variation (Kafkafi et al., 2018; Wahlsten et al., 2003), which may be in part the result of lack of automation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the cause of variation based on the cited literature.

claim: A recent analysis focusing on transgenic mouse models of Alzheimer's disease found a significant amount of variation in the parameters used in the Morris Water Maze.
source: For example, a recent analysis focusing on transgenic mouse models of Alzheimer's disease found a significant amount of variation in the parameters used in the Morris Water Maze, including pool size, pool temperature, number of trials per day, and number of acquisition days (Egan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Egan et al., 2016.

claim: Even when protocol parameters are controlled for, different experimenters can still obtain different behavioural results in conventional behavioural tasks.
source: Further evidence shows that even when protocol parameters are controlled for, different experimenters can still obtain different behavioural results in conventional behavioural tasks (Chesler et al., 2002; Crabbe et al., 1999; Kafkafi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chesler et al., 2002; Crabbe et al., 1999; and Kafkafi et al., 2018.

claim: Non-automated and non-standardised conventional behavioural assessments may be prone to several sources of bias.
source: Overall, there are converging domains of evidence to suggest that non-automated and non-standardised conventional behavioural assessments may be prone to several sources of bias.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature about variability in conventional assessments.

claim: The rodent touchscreen testing method was developed to address gaps in data collection, automation, and translational research.
source: Efforts to address these important gaps in data collection, automation, and translational research led to the development of the rodent touchscreen testing method (Horner et al., 2013; Mar et al., 2013; Oomen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horner et al., 2013; Mar et al., 2013; and Oomen et al., 2013.

claim: Touchscreen technology allows the use of tests in rodents that are highly similar, and in some cases identical, to human cognitive tests.
source: This technology allows the use of tests in rodents that are highly similar, and in some cases identical, to human cognitive tests (Heath et al., 2019; Nilsson et al., 2016; Nithianantharajah et al., 2015; Romberg et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heath et al., 2019; Nilsson et al., 2016; Nithianantharajah et al., 2015; and Romberg et al., 2013a.

claim: Touchscreen testing systems have standardised behavioural protocols that are under the control of a computer system, allowing for increased standardisation of outcomes.
source: Touchscreen testing systems have standardised behavioural protocols that are under the control of a computer system, allowing for increased standardisation of outcomes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about how touchscreen systems operate.

claim: The automation of high-level cognitive testing can provide significant reductions in experimenter and environmental influence.
source: Furthermore, the automation of high-level cognitive testing can provide significant reductions in experimenter and environmental influence, by providing a standard operant environment and standardised output file formats (Horner et al., 2013; Mar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horner et al., 2013 and Mar et al., 2013.

claim: Standardised output file formats make results generated amenable to storage in a central repository, allowing for data categorisation, searching and comparison between multiple laboratories.
source: This feature makes results generated amenable to storage in a central repository, allowing for data categorisation, searching and comparison between multiple laboratories.
evidence: This is an inference about the benefits of standardized formats based on general knowledge of data management.

claim: Data were obtained with male and female mice from three distinct mouse lines commonly used in Alzheimer's disease (AD) research.
source: Here we used data obtained with male and female mice from three distinct mouse lines commonly used in Alzheimer's disease (AD) research to highlight the use of a new repository and Web-based software, MouseBytes (mousebytes.ca).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and data collection in this study.

claim: 3xTG-AD mice, males and females, present early attention deficits (at 3–6 months of age) when compared to their age matched controls.
source: For example, 3xTG-AD mice, males and females, present early attention deficits (at 3–6 months of age) when compared to their age matched controls, demonstrating reproducibility of earlier results.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in the 5-CSRTT results.

claim: The finding of early attention deficits in 3xTG-AD mice demonstrates reproducibility of earlier results.
source: For example, 3xTG-AD mice, males and females, present early attention deficits (at 3–6 months of age) when compared to their age matched controls, demonstrating reproducibility of earlier results.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previously published results (Romberg et al., 2011).

claim: The cognitive assessment suggests which mouse models can be used to model cognitive phenotypes consistent with Alzheimer's disease.
source: Overall, our cognitive assessment suggests which mouse models can be used to model cognitive phenotypes consistent with Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comprehensive cognitive testing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MouseBytes is available to researchers worldwide at mousebytes.ca.
source: MouseBytes is available to researchers worldwide (mousebytes.ca), so they can pre-process, run automated quality control scripts, store, visualise, and analyse their data alone or alongside other researchers' stored data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability and functionality of the MouseBytes platform.

claim: MouseBytes allows researchers to pre-process, run automated quality control scripts, store, visualise, and analyse their data alone or alongside other researchers' stored data.
source: MouseBytes is available to researchers worldwide (mousebytes.ca), so they can pre-process, run automated quality control scripts, store, visualise, and analyse their data alone or alongside other researchers' stored data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functionality of the MouseBytes platform.

claim: Researchers can use a knowledge sharing tool https://touchscreencognition.org to disseminate community-driven information, including standard operating procedures (SOPs) and protocols.
source: Moreover, researchers can use a knowledge sharing tool https://touchscreencognition.org to disseminate community-driven information, including standard operating procedures (SOPs) and protocols.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functionality of the touchscreencognition.org platform.

claim: This repository for touchscreen data is a major step towards increasing the availability of datasets, including negative results.
source: We foresee this repository for touchscreen data as a major step towards increasing the availability of datasets, including negative results, that can serve to evaluate reproducibility, decrease publication bias and to bring high-level cognitive assessment into the Open Science era.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the anticipated impact of the MouseBytes repository.

claim: The repository can serve to evaluate reproducibility, decrease publication bias and to bring high-level cognitive assessment into the Open Science era.
source: We foresee this repository for touchscreen data as a major step towards increasing the availability of datasets, including negative results, that can serve to evaluate reproducibility, decrease publication bias and to bring high-level cognitive assessment into the Open Science era.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the anticipated benefits of the MouseBytes repository.

claim: Data were acquired from male and female mice from three commonly used transgenic mouse models at three ages in two different laboratories on three clinically-relevant touchscreen-based cognitive tests.
source: To highlight the potential strengths of MouseBytes, we acquired data from male and female mice from three commonly used transgenic mouse models that have pathological similarities to AD at three ages in two different laboratories on three clinically-relevant touchscreen-based cognitive tests: attention [5-choice serial reaction time task (5-CSRTT)] (Beraldo et al., 2015; Mar et al., 2013; Romberg et al., 2011), behavioural flexibility [pairwise visual discrimination reversal (PD)] (Bussey et al., 2008; Kolisnyk et al., 2013; Mar et al., 2013) and long-term learning and memory [paired-associates learning (PAL)] (Al-Onaizi et al., 2016; Bartko et al., 2011; Horner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design with supporting citations for each test.

claim: The mouse lines (3xTG-AD, 5xFAD and APP/PS1) were chosen due to their extensive use in AD research.
source: The mouse lines (3xTG-AD, 5xFAD and APP/PS1) were chosen due to their extensive use in AD research, as well as their differences in pathology development and AD familial genetic mutations (Egan et al., 2016; Jankowsky et al., 2004; Lee and Han, 2013; Oakley et al., 2006; Oddo et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations documenting the use and characteristics of these mouse lines.

claim: The mouse lines were chosen due to their differences in pathology development and AD familial genetic mutations.
source: The mouse lines (3xTG-AD, 5xFAD and APP/PS1) were chosen due to their extensive use in AD research, as well as their differences in pathology development and AD familial genetic mutations (Egan et al., 2016; Jankowsky et al., 2004; Lee and Han, 2013; Oakley et al., 2006; Oddo et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations documenting the characteristics of these mouse lines.

claim: The 3xTG-AD mouse line had been tested before using touchscreen attention tests providing a framework for reproducibility testing.
source: Moreover, the 3xTG-AD mouse line had been tested before using touchscreen attention tests providing a framework for reproducibility testing (Romberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Romberg et al., 2011.

claim: XML files were generated using the Animal Behaviour Environment Test II (ABET II by Campden Instruments Ltd, Loughborough, England) software.
source: Following completion of individual experiments, Extensive Markup Language (XML) files were generated using the Animal Behaviour Environment Test II (ABET II by Campden Instruments Ltd, Loughborough, England) software.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection method.

claim: XML files were uploaded into MouseBytes and screened using an automated quality control (QC) procedure.
source: XML files were uploaded into MouseBytes and screened using an automated quality control (QC) procedure which is a tool available at MouseBytes.ca (mousebytesQC).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing pipeline.

claim: The rules and codes for the QC are available for download and modification in GitHub.
source: The rules and codes for the QC are available for download and modification in GitHub (GitHub_Touchscreen_Pipeline; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/Mousebytes-An-open-access-high-throughput-pipeline-and-database-for-rodent-touchscreen-based-data) (Memar et al., 2019) .
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of the QC code.

claim: Files that did not meet the QC criteria were automatically identified.
source: Files that did not meet the QC criteria were automatically identified.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the QC process functionality.

claim: Only XML files that passed QC were automatically uploaded to the database (mousebytes.ca).
source: Following QC, only XML files (one mouse unique ID/session) that passed QC were automatically uploaded to the database (mousebytes.ca) and integrated to the analytics TIBCO Spotfire to generate an interactive visualisation platform for 5-CSRTT, PAL, and PD (Figure 1, see also the online data visualisation - https://mousebytes.ca/data-visualization).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data upload process, with reference to Figure 1 showing the workflow.

claim: XML files that passed QC were integrated to the analytics TIBCO Spotfire to generate an interactive visualisation platform for 5-CSRTT, PAL, and PD.
source: Following QC, only XML files (one mouse unique ID/session) that passed QC were automatically uploaded to the database (mousebytes.ca) and integrated to the analytics TIBCO Spotfire to generate an interactive visualisation platform for 5-CSRTT, PAL, and PD (Figure 1, see also the online data visualisation - https://mousebytes.ca/data-visualization).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data visualization platform, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: A total of 652 different mice were tested.
source: In total, we tested 652 different mice and generated 62,411 xml files (27,440 for 5-CSRTT, 17,230 for PAL, and 17,892 for PD).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size in the study.

claim: 62,411 xml files were generated (27,440 for 5-CSRTT, 17,230 for PAL, and 17,892 for PD).
source: In total, we tested 652 different mice and generated 62,411 xml files (27,440 for 5-CSRTT, 17,230 for PAL, and 17,892 for PD).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the amount of data generated.

claim: 487 files (0.8%) did not meet the QC system criteria.
source: Importantly, by scanning the files through our automated QC procedure, we identified 487 files (0.8%) that did not meet the QC system criteria.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the QC results.

claim: 62,393 xml files (99.2%) passed the automated QC criteria and were transferred to the database.
source: 62,393 xml files (99.2%) passed the automated QC criteria and were transferred to the database.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the QC results.

claim: Classical graphical format to visualise all information contained in these datasets would require close to 30–40 figures with 6–10 panels each.
source: Due to the amount of data we generated in this work, classical graphical format to visualise all information contained in these datasets would require close to 30–40 figures with 6–10 panels each, depending on the kind of comparisons being performed.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the amount of data generated and typical figure formats.

claim: The large amount of data underscores the need for online and on-the-fly data assessment, multidimensional visualisation, and comparison using online visualisation tools.
source: This situation underscores the need for online and on-the-fly data assessment, multidimensional visualisation, and comparison using online visualisation tools (Dunn et al., 2016), such as TIBCO Spotfire (Dunn et al., 2016; Pechter et al., 2016), which we used here.
evidence: This is an inference about the need for online tools, supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2016 and Pechter et al., 2016.

claim: The MouseBytes system has been optimised for the intake of data from the Bussey-Saksida Operant Chamber systems.
source: Currently, our system has been optimised for the intake of data from the Bussey-Saksida Operant Chamber systems (Campden Instruments, Lafayette Instruments).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the current capabilities of the MouseBytes system.

claim: There are alternative commercial touchscreen systems available.
source: There are alternative commercial touchscreen systems available (i.e. Med Associate K-Limbic touchscreen operant chambers), as well as several open source alternatives (O'Leary et al., 2018; Pineño, 2014; Wolf et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Leary et al., 2018; Pineño, 2014; and Wolf et al., 2014.

claim: Codes have been incorporated for download and modification in GitHub to easily convert the formats of output XML files from other systems to the format used in MouseBytes.
source: In order to open the MouseBytes platform to all researchers using touchscreens, we have incorporated codes for download and modification in GitHub (GitHub codes; Memar et al., 2019) to easily convert the formats of output XML files from other systems to the format used in MouseBytes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of conversion codes.

claim: Statistical analysis of the performance of distinct AD mouse models was conducted using R.
source: Statistical analysis of the performance of distinct AD mouse models was conducted using R, taking advantage of the fact that CSV files can be generated for specific datasets using MouseBytes, which facilitates the use of open-source statistical packages.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical analysis methods used.

claim: CSV files can be generated for specific datasets using MouseBytes, which facilitates the use of open-source statistical packages.
source: Statistical analysis of the performance of distinct AD mouse models was conducted using R, taking advantage of the fact that CSV files can be generated for specific datasets using MouseBytes, which facilitates the use of open-source statistical packages.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functionality of MouseBytes.

claim: Variability of mouse performance in behavioural tests across different laboratories is an important issue for replicability.
source: Variability of mouse performance in behavioural tests across different laboratories is an important issue for replicability (Crabbe et al., 1999; Kafkafi et al., 2018; Wahlsten et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Crabbe et al., 1999; Kafkafi et al., 2018; and Wahlsten et al., 2003.

claim: The use of automated and standardized testing can help decrease variability.
source: The use of automated and standardized testing can help decrease variability, although a wide range of factors including colony genetic drift (Zeldovich, 2017), light-dark cycle, types of cages and housing (single housed or group-housed), source of food, type and amount of reward, different types of environmental enrichment and colony room temperature/humidity conditions can still potentially contribute to variability (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations about factors affecting variability.

claim: A wide range of factors can still potentially contribute to variability even with automated testing.
source: The use of automated and standardized testing can help decrease variability, although a wide range of factors including colony genetic drift (Zeldovich, 2017), light-dark cycle, types of cages and housing (single housed or group-housed), source of food, type and amount of reward, different types of environmental enrichment and colony room temperature/humidity conditions can still potentially contribute to variability (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zeldovich, 2017 and Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Site was included as a factor in 5-CSRTT analyses to directly assess potential site variability.
source: To directly assess potential site variability in the current dataset stored in MouseBytes, we included site as a factor in our 5-CSRTT analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical analysis approach.

claim: Throughout the analyses of 5-CSRTT measurements, no consistent pattern of main effects or interactions emerged for site between age, sex, genotype, strain, or measure.
source: Throughout the analyses of 5-CSRTT measurements (see Materials and methods), no consistent pattern of main effects or interactions emerged for site between age, sex, genotype, strain, or measure (stimulus length) (Supplementary file 2, tabs 1, 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis results.

claim: For APP/PS1 mice, only accuracy presented a statistical difference in interactions between test site, genotype, sex, age and stimulus length.
source: For example, for interactions between test site, genotype, sex, age and stimulus length, only APP/PS1 mice presented a statistical difference in accuracy, whereas all other parameters (% correct, number of premature responses, number of perseverative responses, reward collection latency and correct touch latency) for the three strains were not significantly different (Supplementary file 2, tabs 1, 2 and 3, lines 28 #a).
evidence: This is a statement about specific statistical analysis results.

claim: Interactions with test site that were significant typically had a small effect size and lacked consistency across behavioural domains and mouse strains.
source: Interactions with test site that were significant typically had a small effect size and lacked consistency across behavioural domains and mouse strains (Supplementary file 2, tabs 1, 2 and 3, #a).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis results and their interpretation.

claim: The evidence suggests low site-to-site variability and high replicability for touchscreen test performance.
source: Overall, the evidence suggests low site-to-site variability and high replicability for touchscreen test performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis results.

claim: Previous experiments detected robust attentional deficits in 11-month-old male 3xTG-AD mice.
source: Previous experiments have detected robust attentional deficits in 11- month-old male 3xTG-AD mice (Romberg et al., 2011), with lower accuracy in the 5-CSRTT and no differences in omissions compared to wild-type controls (Romberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Romberg et al., 2011.

claim: Male 3xTG-AD mice at 11 months of age reproduced the cognitive signature pattern of attentional deficit as previously published.
source: We tested male 3xTG-AD mice at the same age and reproduced the cognitive signature pattern of attentional deficit as previously published for male mice (Figure 2J, dataset nine for accuracy, Figure 2L, dataset 10 for omissions).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with reference to Figure 2 panels J and L.

claim: Female 3xTG-AD mice presented lower accuracy and no difference in omissions when compared to wild-type controls at 11 months of age.
source: In addition, we also tested female mice and similar to the males, 3xTG-AD female mice also presented lower accuracy (Figure 2N dataset 11) and no difference in omissions (Figure 2P, dataset 12) when compared to the wild-type controls.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with reference to Figure 2 panels N and P.

claim: Both male and female 3xTG-AD mice tested starting at 4 months of age presented lower accuracy and no difference in omissions when compared to controls.
source: Moreover, both male and female 3xTG-AD mice that were tested starting at 4 months of age also presented lower accuracy (Figure 2I, dataset 13 and M, dataset 14) and no difference in omissions (Figure 2K, dataset 15 and 2 O dataset 16) when compared to controls (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 5 - Tab 1, #b).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with references to Figure 2 and supplementary files.

claim: Reduced vigilance was previously reported to be affected in the 3xTG-AD mouse line.
source: We also examined vigilance (the ability to maintain concentrated attention over a prolonged period of time), which was also previously reported to be affected in this mouse line (Romberg et al., 2011), by characterising performance across blocks of 10 trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Romberg et al., 2011.

claim: Reduced vigilance across trials was reflected in a deficit in accuracy in 3xTG-AD males at 10-11 months of age.
source: Reduced vigilance across trials was reflected in a deficit in accuracy in 3xTG-AD males (10–11 month-old mice used as example, Figure 3A–D and Supplementary file 8- Tab 1, #c) or 3xTG- AD female mice (3–6 -month-old mice used as example, Figure 3I–L and Supplementary file 8 - Tab 1, #c).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Reduced vigilance across trials was reflected in a deficit in accuracy in 3xTG-AD females at 3-6 months of age.
source: Reduced vigilance across trials was reflected in a deficit in accuracy in 3xTG-AD males (10–11 month-old mice used as example, Figure 3A–D and Supplementary file 8- Tab 1, #c) or 3xTG- AD female mice (3–6 -month-old mice used as example, Figure 3I–L and Supplementary file 8 - Tab 1, #c).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with reference to Figure 3.

claim: No differences were observed for omissions in vigilance testing of 3xTG-AD mice.
source: No differences were observed for omissions (Figure 3E–H,M–P and Supplementary file 8 – Tab 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with reference to Figure 3.

claim: These experiments support the replicability observed between sites.
source: These experiments support the replicability we observed between sites and suggest that 3xTG-AD mice present robust attentional deficits that can be observed across several laboratories even when a different genetic background is used.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: 3xTG-AD mice present robust attentional deficits that can be observed across several laboratories even when a different genetic background is used.
source: These experiments support the replicability we observed between sites and suggest that 3xTG-AD mice present robust attentional deficits that can be observed across several laboratories even when a different genetic background is used.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and comparison with previous literature.

claim: Genetic drifting can potentially affect reproducibility in mouse behaviour testing.
source: Because genetic drifting can potentially affect reproducibility in mouse behaviour testing (Zeldovich, 2017), identification of robust deficits of high-level cognition resulting from AD-related pathology is important to develop drug treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zeldovich, 2017.

claim: Identification of robust deficits of high-level cognition resulting from AD-related pathology is important to develop drug treatments.
source: Because genetic drifting can potentially affect reproducibility in mouse behaviour testing (Zeldovich, 2017), identification of robust deficits of high-level cognition resulting from AD-related pathology is important to develop drug treatments.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of robust phenotypes for drug development.

claim: Attention deficit in the 3xTG-AD is a robust outcome.
source: It seems that attention deficit in the 3xTG-AD is one such outcome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing consistent attention deficits.

claim: 3xTG-AD male mice showed a small but significant deficit in the PAL task at four months of age.
source: We observed a small but significant deficit in the PAL task for 3xTG-AD male mice at four months of age (Table 2, Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 6 - Tab 1, #d).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results.

claim: 3xTG-AD mice did not show any sign of deficits in visual discrimination learning or behavioural flexibility in PD.
source: 3xTG-AD mice did not show any sign of deficits in visual discrimination learning or behavioural flexibility in PD (Supplementary file 4 and Supplementary file 7 - Tab 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results.

claim: The cognitive phenotype of 3xTG-AD mice resembled patients with early AD, presenting early deficits in sustained attention and visual-spatial learning, but not in behavioural flexibility.
source: Overall, the cognitive phenotype of these mice resembled patients with early AD, presenting early deficits in sustained attention (Perry et al., 2000) and visual-spatial learning (Blackwell et al., 2004), but not in behavioural flexibility (Sahakian et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and comparison with human AD literature.

claim: The 5xFAD mice were used in a mixed genetic background (C57Bl6 and Swiss Jim Lambert -SJL), as this was the original background in which this mouse line was generated.
source: We chose to use the 5xFAD mice in a mixed genetic background (C57Bl6 and Swiss Jim Lambert -SJL), as this was the original background in which this mouse line was generated (Oakley et al., 2006), and it is the most commonly used background across several laboratories (Qosa and Kaddoumi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oakley et al., 2006 and Qosa and Kaddoumi, 2016.

claim: The SJL genetic background presents the Pdebrd1 mutation that can lead to retinal degeneration.
source: However, the SJL genetic background presents the Pdebrd1 mutation that can lead to retinal degeneration (Clapcote et al., 2005) (see Materials and methods), which causes severe visual impairment in homozygosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Clapcote et al., 2005.

claim: The Pdebrd1 mutation causes severe visual impairment in homozygosis.
source: However, the SJL genetic background presents the Pdebrd1 mutation that can lead to retinal degeneration (Clapcote et al., 2005) (see Materials and methods), which causes severe visual impairment in homozygosis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the Pdebrd1 mutation.

claim: The performance of mice carrying one Pdebrd allele did not differ from those who did not in the PD task.
source: The performance of mice carrying one Pdebrd allele did not differ from those who did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B and C).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No differences were found in amyloid production and deposition between food restricted and non-food restricted animals.
source: Ultimately, we failed to find any differences in amyloid production and deposition between food restricted and non-food restricted animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
